an3.37:1.1: In [dn32](), the four great kings are named Dhataraṭṭha lord of centaurs in the east, Virūḷha lord of gnomes in the south, Virūpakkha lord of dragons in the west, and Kuvera Vessavaṇa lord of native spirits in Uttarakuru in the north. | Yama, in thinking of committing a misdeed, is all too aware of this constant surveillance: “They do not stand still; they do not blink—the spies of the gods who roam about here” (Rig Veda 10.10.8).
an3.37:1.2: _Paṭijāgaronti_ (= BHSK _pratijāgarti_) means “to wakefully watch over”, i.e. “keep vigil”. In the Buddhist tradition of north-east Thailand, it is still a common practice to remain awake the whole night for the _uposatha_. | According to Śathapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.1.4, “the gods know the minds of man, so they are aware that his fire-oblation is to take place on the next day. The gods go there and stay (_upa-vas_) in his house, which is why this day is called _upavasatha_”. For more on the sabbath, see [an3.70]() and notes.
an3.37:1.3: Each of the four great kings is said to have many sons, all named Indra ([dn20](), [dn32]()).
an3.37:1.5: From emissaries, to sons, to the four great kings themselves, those who wander are graded to match the significance of the sabbaths on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days respectively. How the calendar works is this. There are three seasons—hot, rainy, and cold—each of four months (a leap month is added to the hot season every few years). Each season has eight fortnights of fifteen days, except the third and seventh, which are fourteen days. These are the fifteenth and fourteenth day sabbaths, while the eighth day sabbaths fall on the week in-between. The days of most significance, such as start of the season, always fall on the fifteenth day.
an3.37:1.6: Notice the excellent management strategy of the four great kings. They trust their emissaries, but vary the responsibility with their even more trusted sons, and for the times of most importance, are present themselves.
an3.37:2.2: The gods of the four great kings, and their delegated proxies, are acting as an intermediary to the gods of the thirty-three, who occupy a higher celestial plane. They are divine messengers of a sort, but their message is for the gods rather than the humans.
an3.37:2.5: The endless struggle between gods and titans reflects their sources in nature. The gods (_deva_) stem from Proto Indo-European _*dyew_, “shining, sky, heavens” (cf. Pali _diva_, “day”; English “day”, however, is a false friend), while the titans (_asura_) are the negative form of Proto Indo-European _*sóh₂wl_, “sun”, so _asura_ is “sunless, night”. As the day vanquishes the dark of night each dawn, the gods defeat the titans. Victory is sweet but short-lived, for soon follows dusk, at which the titans prevail and plunge the world into darkness once more (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.5.1, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.9.7). For more, see [sn11.1]() and  [sn11.5]().
an3.37:5.6: The meaning of _pāṭihāriyapakkha_ is uncertain, and the translation “extraordinary fortnight” is a guess. _Pakkha_ is fortnight. _Pāṭihāriya_ normally means “demonstration”, something that is apt to captivate or win over an audience ([dn11:3.8}()). It is not clear how this meaning applies here. The commentaries are inconsistent, sometimes saying this is a special _uposatha_ during the rains, and sometimes saying it refers to keeping the precepts on extra days before or after the normal one; this, however, depends on adopting a reading not found in the text, as it glosses _pāṭihāriya_ with _pariharitabba_. There does not seem to be any trace of a corresponding term in Vedic texts.
